1.pericope_label: Now these are the words of the letter that Jeremiah the prophet sent from Jerusalem unto the residue of the elders which were carried away captives, and to the priests, and to the prophets, and to all the people whom Nebuchadnezzar had carried away captive from Jerusalem to Babylon; (After that Jeconiah the king, and the queen, and the eunuchs, the princes of Judah and Jerusalem, and the carpenters, and the smiths, were departed from Jerusalem;) By the hand of Elasah the son of Shaphan, and Gemariah the son of Hilkiah, (whom Zedekiah king of Judah sent unto Babylon to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon) saying,

schools.summary: Ellicott sets the letter against a restless disquietude among the first exiles fostered by prophets urging revolt, identifies the queen as the queen-mother and the two messengers as men from families friendly to the prophet, infers from the sending of envoys that the king had half abandoned revolt, and notes that the shorter spelling of the prophet's name in the opening verse probably marks that sentence as a later hand's.

Gill observes that prophets taught by epistle as well as by sermon, as the apostles afterwards did. Calvin gives the letter a double design, to lighten the grief of the exiles and to break the obstinacy of those still at home who thought themselves fortunate to have escaped, and sums the counsel as looking to the end of the captivity while raising no tumults meanwhile.

Clarke summarises the chapter as two letters, dates it to the first or second year of Zedekiah, and explains that the prophet feared the deported would take some hasty step on the strength of promises of a quick return. Wesley distinguishes two deportations eleven or twelve years apart, assigns this to the earlier, and explains that the prophet used the king's embassy to quiet minds unsettled by flatterers in both cities.

Henry makes the writing of the letter itself the lesson, that what is written is as truly inspired as what is spoken and that we may serve God by writing to distant friends what we cannot say to them; he lists the classes carried away, notes that removing the carpenters and smiths left the city unable to arm itself, and remarks that a surrender meant to pacify the conqueror only made him grow on their concessions.

debates.question: What was the letter written to accomplish?

positions.position: An earnest protest against the policy of revolt urged by false prophets among the exiles.
To prevent hasty action by men persuaded they would soon be brought home.
Both to comfort the exiles and to break the obstinacy of those still in Judea, who needed to learn that joining their brethren would suit them best.
To comfort captives who, being singled out, looked to others like the greater sinners.

debates.question: What can be inferred from the messengers who carried it?

positions.position: That the king had been influenced by the prophet's counsel, had half abandoned revolt and was acknowledging Babylon's overlordship, since a letter carried by royal envoys is unlikely to have contradicted their mission.
Only that the king had occasion to send two messengers and the prophet used the opportunity.

outliers.claim: Argues from the shorter spelling of the prophet's name in the opening verse, against the form used throughout the rest of the book, that the sentence introducing the letter was probably the work of a later hand.

Draws a rule of correspondence from the fact of a written prophecy: what is written is as truly given by inspiration as what is spoken, and we may serve God by writing to distant friends what we cannot say, since what is written remains.

themes: Now these are the words of the letter that Jeremiah the prophet sent from Jerusalem unto the residue of the elders which were carried away captives, and to the priests, and to the prophets, and to all the people whom Nebuchadnezzar had carried away captive from Jerusalem to Babylon;
(After that Jeconiah the king, and the queen, and the eunuchs, the princes of Judah and Jerusalem, and the carpenters, and the smiths, were departed from Jerusalem;)
By the hand of Elasah the son of Shaphan, and Gemariah the son of Hilkiah, (whom Zedekiah king of Judah sent unto Babylon to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon) saying,

4.pericope_label: Thus saith the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, unto all that are carried away captives, whom I have caused to be carried away from Jerusalem unto Babylon; Build ye houses, and dwell in them; and plant gardens, and eat the fruit of them; Take ye wives, and beget sons and daughters; and take wives for your sons, and give your daughters to husbands, that they may bear sons and daughters; that ye may be increased there, and not diminished. And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the Lord for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.

schools.summary: Ellicott treats the passage as the nearest thing in the older scriptures to an apostolic epistle, gives the command to build a twofold bearing of patient acceptance and a two-generation term, infers comparative leniency from the exiles being allowed to own land, and calls the order to seek the city's peace the hardest command in the letter, concluding that the imprecations of the psalm of the willows belong to a lower stage than this counsel.

Gill attends to the divine titles the letter opens with and to the manner of the seeking, and reads the marriage clause as forbidding intermarriage with the Chaldeans. Calvin resolves the apparent contradiction between settling down and hoping for return by assigning obedience and hope different offices, guards the counsel against both indulgence and impatience, and settles the disputed verb by parallels in which seeking means caring for and promoting.

Clarke reads the command as preparation for a long stay and multiplication into a powerful people, and defends the order to seek the city's peace on grounds of plain interest, since wherever a man lives and is fed is his country while he stays, and these exiles were better placed than the brethren they had left.

debates.question: Does seeking the peace of the city mean praying for it or working for it?

positions.position: Chiefly active effort for the safety of the monarchy, the verb meaning to care for and promote as in parallel idioms, with prayer following after.
Both together: prayer and every other useful means.
Promoting the prosperity of the place, letting no disaffection appear in word or act.
Praying for the prosperity of the city, which required a patience close to superhuman.

debates.question: How can settling in Chaldea be consistent with hoping for return?

positions.position: Obedience and hope occupy different offices: obedience submits for the whole term, hope hangs in suspense so that they neither fret nor are carried away.
The command simply counsels patient acceptance while announcing a term of at least two generations.
It is preparation for a long continuance, with a view to becoming a powerful people.

outliers.claim: Concludes that unless one distinguishes the times and dates it differently, the imprecations of the psalm sung by the waters of Babylon belong to a lower stage of spiritual progress than this letter's counsel, and sets the prophet beside the charge to pray for an emperor who was Nero.
Warns that a man driven headlong by vehement desire in a manner repels God's favour, taking from him his rights and will, as though unwilling to receive the grace at all.

themes: Thus saith the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, unto all that are carried away captives, whom I have caused to be carried away from Jerusalem unto Babylon;
Build ye houses, and dwell in them; and plant gardens, and eat the fruit of them;

Take ye wives, and beget sons and daughters; and take wives for your sons, and give your daughters to husbands, that they may bear sons and daughters; that ye may be increased there, and not diminished.
And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the Lord for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.

8.pericope_label: For thus saith the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel; Let not your prophets and your diviners, that be in the midst of you, deceive you, neither hearken to your dreams which ye cause to be dreamed. For they prophesy falsely unto you in my name: I have not sent them, saith the Lord. For thus saith the Lord, That after seventy years be accomplished at Babylon I will visit you, and perform my good word toward you, in causing you to return to this place. For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, saith the Lord, thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end.

schools.summary: Ellicott sees the same agencies at work in Babylon as at Jerusalem, calls the dreams which ye cause to be dreamed an exceptional phrase indicating that the supply was created by the demand, and rejects the familiar rendering expected end for a future and a hope, which he says is what the words literally mean and is far more expressive, since an expected end may be one a man shrinks from.

Gill grounds the seventy years in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, notes that the false prophets' pretence of divine authority was what made them credible, and dwells on the security of a purpose held in God's mind, since men think and forget while his thoughts cannot fail. Calvin explains the length of the promise by the two extremes men fall into, vain confidence and dead despair, both of which this people had shown.

Clarke would render dreamers rather than dreams, makes the seventy years a measure that must be filled to the brim before any enlargement, sets the promise out as a numbered scheme turning on seeking God with the whole heart, and reports a proposed transposition of the chapter's verses without adopting it. Wesley dates the term from the first deportation and concludes that eleven years had already run, and takes the promised end as the very end the exiles expect and desire.

Henry holds that so long as we have the word of truth to try the spirits by, being deceived is our own fault, and works the causative in the dreams clause both ways, as the people's own waking fancies carried into sleep and as the prophets' dreams which the people wanted; false prophets, he concludes, would not flatter men in their sins if men did not love it.

debates.question: Should the word be rendered dreams or dreamers?

positions.position: Dreamers, there being a class of men skilled in the practice who also interpreted for others.
Dreams, the causative form being the point: the supply was created by the demand for such visions.
Dreams, either the people's own fancies or the prophets', called theirs because they wanted them.

debates.question: How should an expected end be rendered?

positions.position: A future and a hope, which is the literal sense and far more expressive, since an expected end may be one a man shrinks from.
The end they themselves expect and desire, grounded on mercy to the seed of Abraham rather than merit.

debates.question: From when are the seventy years counted?

positions.position: From the fourth year of Jehoiakim, when the conqueror first came against the city; not from the last captivity, the present moment, or the first deportation.
From the same first carrying away, so that eleven years had already elapsed.
The words fix a measure to be filled to the brim; the whole term must be completed and no enlargement looked for.

outliers.claim: Reports a proposal that a very serious transposition of verses has occurred in the chapter, so that after the ninth verse one should read the sixteenth through the nineteenth, then the tenth through the fourteenth, then the twentieth, the fifteenth and the twenty-first; he records it without adopting it.

Explains the length of the promise by a diagnosis of two extremes: men are either rapt above the clouds by vain hopes or lie astonished in despair, and this people showed both, laughing at threatenings at home and then in exile believing anyone who promised a quick return.

themes: For thus saith the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel; Let not your prophets and your diviners, that be in the midst of you, deceive you, neither hearken to your dreams which ye cause to be dreamed.
For they prophesy falsely unto you in my name: I have not sent them, saith the Lord.
For thus saith the Lord, That after seventy years be accomplished at Babylon I will visit you, and perform my good word toward you, in causing you to return to this place.
For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, saith the Lord, thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end.

12.pericope_label: Then shall ye call upon me, and ye shall go and pray unto me, and I will hearken unto you. And ye shall seek me, and find me, when ye shall search for me with all your heart. And I will be found of you, saith the Lord: and I will turn away your captivity, and I will gather you from all the nations, and from all the places whither I have driven you, saith the Lord; and I will bring you again into the place whence I caused you to be carried away captive.

schools.summary: Ellicott refers the substance and fulfilment of the promised restoration to his notes on an earlier chapter without expanding it here.

Gill makes the spirit of prayer a gift given when God means to bestow the mercy, so that the promise itself is an argument for praying, and sets out at length what seeking rightly involves: in Christ, under the Spirit, in the exercise of faith, with fervency, diligence and sincerity. Calvin rejects the moral reading of the middle verb that almost all adopt, identifies seeking with praying, extends the promise from Israel to the whole church, and distinguishes hiding from manifestation in the promised gathering.
Clarke identifies the promise to gather them as a quotation from the older law rather than a new saying.

debates.question: What does the verb for going or walking mean here?

positions.position: A right course of life, the men who wandered after their lusts now walking in the law; this is what almost all take it to mean.
Too forced a reading: it is an indirect reproof of their slowness, meaning that after seventy years and not one they will at last begin to be wise.

debates.question: Should the particle before the whole-heart clause be when or because?

positions.position: Because is the usual sense and may stand, sincerity being justly given as the reason prayers are heard rather than a condition attached.

debates.question: What does seeking and finding consist in?

positions.position: Prayer, as the Lord's own exhortation to seek and knock shows; and the promise reaches the whole church, not the exiles only.
Seeking in Christ under the Spirit's guidance, in faith, with fervency, diligence and sincerity; where those conditions are met men always find him.

outliers.claim: Sets a contrast between hiding and manifestation: God had in a manner hidden himself through the exile, and though he looks on us always we think him far off until we perceive that he is caring for our salvation.

Notes that the promise to gather them was framed to meet an obvious doubt, since they had no region allotted them in which to live together as one body but had been driven apart like chaff before a whirlwind.

themes: Then shall ye call upon me, and ye shall go and pray unto me, and I will hearken unto you.
And ye shall seek me, and find me, when ye shall search for me with all your heart.

And I will be found of you, saith the Lord: and I will turn away your captivity, and I will gather you from all the nations, and from all the places whither I have driven you, saith the Lord; and I will bring you again into the place whence I caused you to be carried away captive.

15.pericope_label: Because ye have said, The Lord hath raised us up prophets in Babylon; Know that thus saith the Lord of the king that sitteth upon the throne of David, and of all the people that dwelleth in this city, and of your brethren that are not gone forth with you into captivity; Thus saith the Lord of hosts; Behold, I will send upon them the sword, the famine, and the pestilence, and will make them like vile figs, that cannot be eaten, they are so evil. And I will persecute them with the sword, with the famine, and with the pestilence, and will deliver them to be removed to all the kingdoms of the earth, to be a curse, and an astonishment, and an hissing, and a reproach, among all the nations whither I have driven them: Because they have not hearkened to my words, saith the Lord, which I sent unto them by my servants the prophets, rising up early and sending them; but ye would not hear, saith the Lord.

schools.summary: Ellicott takes the verse for the exiles' boast that they had prophets of their own, and reads the answer as a contrast between the exiles in whom the nation's hope lies and the worthless king and people left behind; he also notes that the vile figs are borrowed from an earlier vision but that the word here is a different and stronger one, meaning horrible or loathsome.

Gill marks the turn from the godly among the captives to those who believed the flatterers, and draws the inference that the men at Jerusalem would soon be captives beside them or dead. Calvin explains why the discourse turns to the king at all, distinguishes two senses of sitting, and shows that the throne was the very thing on which the exiles hung their hope, since kingdom and priesthood together seemed to guarantee the nation.

Clarke frames the passage as advice not to envy the king or the people left in the land, since sword, pestilence and famine are coming on them, while the exiles have already seen the worst of their case and hold a promise of enlargement at the proper time.

Henry supplies the complaint the letter met, that its writer was making himself busy among men satisfied with prophets of their own, and calls it impudence that the people who invited the flattery fathered it on God, since anyone who hardens men in their sins with groundless hopes is no prophet of God's raising up.

debates.question: Why does the letter turn from the exiles to the king and people at home?

positions.position: To set the exiles, in whom the nation's future hope lies, against the worthless remnant for whom sharper suffering is foretold.
So the captives might see the madness of promising themselves a return when final ruin stood near both king and people.
As advice not to envy those left behind, the exiles having seen the worst of their own case.
To show that those at Jerusalem would soon be captives beside them or destroyed.

debates.question: Why is the throne expressly mentioned?

positions.position: Because the exiles hung their hope on it, reasoning that while temple and kingdom stood it could not be over with the nation; only when that splendour was extinguished could they be humbled.

outliers.claim: Reports that the Greek version places this verse between the twentieth and twenty-first, which he says leaves the connection here undisturbed and completes the connection below; it is the second dislocation of the order he records in this chapter.

Holds as a standing principle that the prophets drew the substance of their doctrine from the law and brought nothing strictly new, accommodating it to their own times, and applies it to the curses named here; he also prefers to read the nations as shaking the head in contempt rather than trembling at the spectacle.

themes: Because ye have said, The Lord hath raised us up prophets in Babylon;

Know that thus saith the Lord of the king that sitteth upon the throne of David, and of all the people that dwelleth in this city, and of your brethren that are not gone forth with you into captivity;
Thus saith the Lord of hosts; Behold, I will send upon them the sword, the famine, and the pestilence, and will make them like vile figs, that cannot be eaten, they are so evil.

And I will persecute them with the sword, with the famine, and with the pestilence, and will deliver them to be removed to all the kingdoms of the earth, to be a curse, and an astonishment, and an hissing, and a reproach, among all the nations whither I have driven them:
Because they have not hearkened to my words, saith the Lord, which I sent unto them by my servants the prophets, rising up early and sending them; but ye would not hear, saith the Lord.

20.pericope_label: Hear ye therefore the word of the Lord, all ye of the captivity, whom I have sent from Jerusalem to Babylon: Thus saith the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, of Ahab the son of Kolaiah, and of Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah, which prophesy a lie unto you in my name; Behold, I will deliver them into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon; and he shall slay them before your eyes; And of them shall be taken up a curse by all the captivity of Judah which are in Babylon, saying, The Lord make thee like Zedekiah and like Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire; Because they have committed villany in Israel, and have committed adultery with their neighbours’ wives, and have spoken lying words in my name, which I have not commanded them; even I know, and am a witness, saith the Lord.

schools.summary: Ellicott generalises the curse-formula into a habit of the language, the tendency to seize on individual cases of the highest blessedness or deepest shame and work them into set forms; he notes that the noun rendered villainy is almost always used of sins of impurity, and suggests that the stress on God's knowledge answers men who had persuaded themselves that he hardly exercised his power so far off as Babylon.

Gill separates the crimes named in the text from the king's motive for the burning, reporting a tradition about the king's daughter and thinking the real provocation was their prophesying Babylon's immediate fall; he lists adultery and false prophesying as the folly meant. Calvin makes the manner of the death the proof of the prophecy, since anyone might have supposed the men would be killed and nobody that they would be roasted.

Clarke reports a division of the chapter into two letters, the second beginning at the fifteenth verse, and supplies a political motive for the king, whose Israelite subjects were made restless by predictions of deliverance; he adds that burning alive was a Chaldean punishment other nations borrowed, and the rabbinic identification of the pair with the two elders of the Susanna story.

Henry arranges the guilt in ascending order, lying being bad, lying to God's people to delude them worse, and resting their own lies on the God of truth worst of all; he explains the motive as flattery offered because the flatterers could not reprove others without condemning themselves, and ends on the day that will bring the hidden works of darkness to light.

debates.question: Why were the two prophets put to death?

positions.position: For political reasons: their predictions made the king's Israelite subjects restless and might have provoked revolt.
Probably for prophesying Babylon's immediate fall and stirring the captives to prepare for home; the crimes named in the text are what moved God to hand them over, not what moved the king.

debates.question: Why is the manner of the death specified?

positions.position: Because it is the proof of prophecy: the death alone might have been guessed, the roasting could not, so the prophet points as with a finger at something incredible.

debates.question: What is the force of the charge translated villany?

positions.position: Folly, meaning the adultery and the false prophesying named after it.
A noun almost always used of sins of impurity and more commonly rendered folly, the English villainy carrying that sense for an older writer.

outliers.claim: Suggests that the emphasis on God knowing and witnessing answers false prophets whose narrow idea of God had persuaded them that he hardly exercised his power in a place as distant as Babylon, where they might sin undetected.

Notes that the verb behind the roasting is rendered fried by the versions, appears nowhere else in Hebrew as a verb, and has a participle used of parched corn; and distinguishes the word for cursing here from the word for an oath used just before.

themes: Hear ye therefore the word of the Lord, all ye of the captivity, whom I have sent from Jerusalem to Babylon:

Thus saith the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, of Ahab the son of Kolaiah, and of Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah, which prophesy a lie unto you in my name; Behold, I will deliver them into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon; and he shall slay them before your eyes;
And of them shall be taken up a curse by all the captivity of Judah which are in Babylon, saying, The Lord make thee like Zedekiah and like Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire;

Because they have committed villany in Israel, and have committed adultery with their neighbours’ wives, and have spoken lying words in my name, which I have not commanded them; even I know, and am a witness, saith the Lord.

24.pericope_label: Thus shalt thou also speak to Shemaiah the Nehelamite, saying, Thus speaketh the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, saying, Because thou hast sent letters in thy name unto all the people that are at Jerusalem, and to Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah the priest, and to all the priests, saying, The Lord hath made thee priest in the stead of Jehoiada the priest, that ye should be officers in the house of the Lord, for every man that is mad, and maketh himself a prophet, that thou shouldest put him in prison, and in the stocks. Now therefore why hast thou not reproved Jeremiah of Anathoth, which maketh himself a prophet to you? For therefore he sent unto us in Babylon, saying, This captivity is long: build ye houses, and dwell in them; and plant gardens, and eat the fruit of them. And Zephaniah the priest read this letter in the ears of Jeremiah the prophet.

schools.summary: Ellicott marks these verses off as a fragment attached to the letter rather than part of it, giving the sequel of events; he explains the deputy priest's duty to punish pretenders to prophecy and reads his known conduct as a deliberately neutral position open to threats, and points out that the word captivity has nothing answering to it in the Hebrew, so that the clause may mean simply that everything is far off.

Gill notes that the whole blame is laid on the priests, who on the accuser's showing should have stopped the prophet's mouth and prevented the letter. Calvin hears in the appeal a charge of ingratitude against a man promoted beyond hope, draws the moral that Satan's ministers turn themselves into angels of light without being able to imitate God's servants closely, and defends the accused, whose design was not to make the captives careless but to keep them from anticipating the promises.

Clarke identifies the addressee as the second priest and records his death at Riblah after the city fell, and glosses the word rendered mad as the ecstatic rapture that came on prophets true or false. Wesley identifies the same office and takes the reference to the predecessor as meaning that the man should be like that good high priest.

Henry observes that the accuser neither defended his own commission nor argued for his predictions but wrote to the priests and set them on to persecute, in his own name and by the very messengers who had brought the letter he was answering; he reads the reference to the predecessor as flattery, presses the injustice of throwing the false prophets' character on the true, and thinks the deputy protected the prophet by showing him the letters.

debates.question: What does the description attached to Shemaiah's name mean?

positions.position: Nothing can be got from it, since no place of that name occurs; at most there may be a play on the Hebrew for dreamer.
The man is the dreamer, since he claimed to receive all his prophecies in dreams.

debates.question: How should the complaint about the length of the exile be read?

positions.position: The word captivity is not in the Hebrew; the clause may mean it is far off, either because the writer relied on Babylon's distance or as an abrupt summary that exile's end and homeland are alike remote.
In the received sense; and the accusation turns round, since those who had said the captivity would never come were already proved liars.

debates.question: How did Zephaniah act on the letters?

positions.position: Not as the writer wished, using them at most as a warning, which agrees with his character elsewhere.
He protected the prophet and read him the contents so that he might know what enemies he had among the captives.

outliers.claim: Reports a division of the chapter into two separate letters, the second beginning at the fifteenth verse and continuing from the twenty-first, which is the third rearrangement of the order he records here without adopting one.

Draws from the accuser's flattery the moral that Satan's ministers transform themselves into angels of light but cannot imitate God's servants closely, since craft is a very different thing from prudent counsel.

themes: Thus shalt thou also speak to Shemaiah the Nehelamite, saying,

Thus speaketh the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, saying, Because thou hast sent letters in thy name unto all the people that are at Jerusalem, and to Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah the priest, and to all the priests, saying,

The Lord hath made thee priest in the stead of Jehoiada the priest, that ye should be officers in the house of the Lord, for every man that is mad, and maketh himself a prophet, that thou shouldest put him in prison, and in the stocks.
Now therefore why hast thou not reproved Jeremiah of Anathoth, which maketh himself a prophet to you?
For therefore he sent unto us in Babylon, saying, This captivity is long: build ye houses, and dwell in them; and plant gardens, and eat the fruit of them.
And Zephaniah the priest read this letter in the ears of Jeremiah the prophet.

30.pericope_label: Then came the word of the Lord unto Jeremiah, saying, Send to all them of the captivity, saying, Thus saith the Lord concerning Shemaiah the Nehelamite; Because that Shemaiah hath prophesied unto you, and I sent him not, and he caused you to trust in a lie: Therefore thus saith the Lord; Behold, I will punish Shemaiah the Nehelamite, and his seed: he shall not have a man to dwell among this people; neither shall he behold the good that I will do for my people, saith the Lord; because he hath taught rebellion against the Lord.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch state the two limbs of the sentence plainly, that none of the man's children shall be left among the people and that he shall not share in the good the Lord will yet do, both being the penalty of rebellion against a commandment. Ellicott takes the command to send as implying a further letter carried by envoys, treats the preservation of the prediction as implying its fulfilment, and finds the frequency of traffic between the two cities worth noticing for what it settles elsewhere in the book.

Gill grounds the sentence in prophesying unsent and prophesying lies, and notes that the word came immediately after the letter was read aloud. Calvin makes the brevity of the oracle its point, since a herald proclaiming judgment does not argue; he observes that childlessness was a curse named in the law, reads the exclusion as an exact reciprocity for despising the appointed time, and draws the doctrine that nothing is more pestiferous in a church than a false confidence.

Clarke divides the punishment into three, no posterity to succeed him, no relations among those brought back, and no sight of the good himself, and names the offence as exciting the people to reject the true prophet and receive the lying words of the false.

debates.question: How many parts has the sentence?

positions.position: Two: the extinction of his line and his exclusion from the day of redemption.
Three: no posterity to succeed him, no relations among the returning, and no sight of the good himself.

debates.question: Why is the oracle so short?

positions.position: Because a herald proclaiming judgment does not argue; the brevity is deliberate, and the more striking against an impostor who carried himself high.

debates.question: Was the prediction fulfilled?

positions.position: No record survives, but its preservation implies fulfilment.
The sentence did no good to the man or his posterity; its use was to work on the exiles and bring them to repentance.

outliers.claim: Reads the second half of the sentence as an exact reciprocity: the man wanted to be home in two years where the prophet commanded patience to the end of seventy, and for despising the appointed time he is shut out from ever seeing it arrive.

Finds the frequency of communication between Jerusalem and Babylon worth noticing in itself, both as supporting a literal reading of an earlier journey in the book and as helping to account for the particular orders later given about the prophet's treatment when the city fell.

themes: Then came the word of the Lord unto Jeremiah, saying,

Send to all them of the captivity, saying, Thus saith the Lord concerning Shemaiah the Nehelamite; Because that Shemaiah hath prophesied unto you, and I sent him not, and he caused you to trust in a lie:

Therefore thus saith the Lord; Behold, I will punish Shemaiah the Nehelamite, and his seed: he shall not have a man to dwell among this people; neither shall he behold the good that I will do for my people, saith the Lord; because he hath taught rebellion against the Lord.
